title: Stoicism · Episode 1
chapters: Stoicism today: an ancient philosophy goes viral

units.t: Stoicism. Episode one.
In this episode: Stoicism today: an ancient philosophy goes viral, Zeno and the painted porch and Epictetus: freedom in the mind.
Part one. Stoicism today: an ancient philosophy goes viral.
Footballers, generals and millions of readers have rediscovered a 2,300-year-old philosophy.
Here's where it shows up now, and what people get wrong about it.
Classrooms to bestsellers.
For most of the 20th century, Stoicism lived in university classics departments.
Then it spread fast.
In 2009 the American philosopher William Irvine published A Guide to the Good Life, pitching Stoicism as a practical philosophy for ordinary people.
In 2014 the marketer turned writer Ryan Holiday released The Obstacle Is the Way, its title adapted from a line of Marcus Aurelius.
A daily newsletter, a podcast and more books followed.
Massimo Pigliucci's How to Be a Stoic and Donald Robertson's How to Think Like a Roman Emperor added to the boom.
The ancient teachers themselves appear in later lessons.
Locker rooms and uniforms.
Sport has embraced Stoicism.
Holiday's book, about treating setbacks as raw material, spread through American football.

Staff at the New England Patriots reportedly read it in their 2014 season, which ended in a Super Bowl win, and Seattle Seahawks coach Pete Carroll and general manager John Schneider are said to have passed it around too.
Athletes can't control referees, injuries or weather, and dwelling on them wastes energy.
Military culture prizes endurance and calm under fire.
Former US general and defence secretary Jim Mattis has described carrying Marcus Aurelius's Meditations on deployments.
The philosopher Nancy Sherman, in Stoic Warriors, 2005, admired this but warned that prizing calm over fear and grief can push people to bury pain.
Veterans, she argues, need room to feel and talk, not just endure.
Small-s stoicism.
Psychologists separate capital-S Stoicism, the philosophy, from small-s stoicism: hiding feelings, enduring pain without complaint and insisting on handling everything alone.
Studies link small-s stoicism with people, especially men, delaying a visit to the doctor or help for their mental health, including research on men in rural Australia.
The irony is that the ancient Stoics constantly sought counsel.
Seneca's letters show one friend helping another through fear, illness and grief, and Stoic students trained with teachers.
The 'stiff upper lip' isn't the goal either.
Despite its British image, the phrase's earliest known use is in an American newspaper in 1815.
Seething behind a brave face is not the Stoic work, which happens in how you think about events.
If you're ignoring chest pain or struggling in silence, see a doctor or ask for help early.
The case against.
Not everyone welcomes the revival.
Critics use the jokey term 'broicism' for online versions that sell Stoicism to ambitious young men as a kit of cold showers, grinding and never showing feelings.
The classicist Donna Zuckerberg's 2018 book Not All Dead White Men documented how parts of the online 'manosphere' borrowed Stoic writers to justify contempt for women and emotion.
Others argue that a narrow focus on your own reactions can slide into shrugging at injustice, although the ancient Stoics insisted on public duty.
Pop versions also drop the Stoic idea of a rational, ordered universe, which made acceptance make sense to the ancients.
Whether the ethics works without it is still debated.
Test it yourself.
In 2012 classicists, philosophers and psychotherapists at the University of Exeter ran a trial: could ordinary people benefit from living like a Stoic for a week?
Stoic Week became an annual event, usually in October.
Tens of thousands have joined.
Participants typically report higher life satisfaction and fewer negative emotions afterwards.
Treat that with care: they are keen volunteers, many drop out before the final survey, and there's no comparison group.
You can run your own experiment.
Each evening for a week, rate your calm, mood and coping from 1 to 10.
Each morning, try one practice from the Stoic practices lesson.
Then see which helped.
Simply paying attention to your mood can lift it, so treat the results as a personal guide, not proof.
The key idea: Once confined to classics departments, Stoicism became one of the most popular philosophies of the 21st century.
Part two. Zeno and the painted porch.
A shipwrecked merchant walked into an Athens bookshop, and a philosophy was born that would guide emperors and slaves alike.
Shipwreck and porch.
Zeno was a merchant from Citium, on Cyprus.
According to the biographer Diogenes Laertius, a shipwreck near Athens, traditionally dated around 312 BC, cost him a cargo of purple dye.
In an Athens bookshop he heard about Socrates and asked where men like that could be found.
The bookseller pointed to the philosopher Crates and said, 'Follow that man.'
Zeno later joked, 'I made a prosperous voyage when I was shipwrecked.'
The details may be embroidered, but the moral stuck: disaster can start something better.
Around 300 BC, Zeno began teaching in the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch, a public colonnade by the Athenian marketplace.
His followers became known as Stoics, 'the porch people'.
Cynics and virtue.
Crates was a Cynic, one of Athens' most provocative groups.
Their best-known figure, Diogenes, reportedly lived in a large storage jar, owned almost nothing and mocked wealth and fame.
Crates gave away his fortune to live likewise.
From them Zeno learned that happiness doesn't depend on possessions or status.
The Stoics kept the core but dropped the shock tactics: you could live virtuously while marrying, working and taking part in public life.
The Stoics said the only true good is virtue: wisdom, justice, courage and self-control.
Health, wealth, reputation and even life are 'indifferent'.
Not worthless: they are 'preferred indifferents', sensible to pursue, but they do not decide whether your life goes well.
What matters is how you use what you're dealt.
Nature and emotions.
Zeno taught that the goal is to live in agreement with nature.
The universe is ordered by reason, which Stoics called logos.
Humans are rational, social beings, so living naturally meant using reason well and serving the human community.
Stoics were early cosmopolitans, 'citizens of the world', picturing concern spreading outward from self and family to all of humanity.
A common myth is that Stoics wanted to feel nothing.
They targeted the passions: fear, craving, distress and excessive pleasure, which grow from false judgements, such as thinking a loss of money is a genuine catastrophe.
Correct the judgement and the passion weakens.
They welcomed good feelings such as joy and goodwill.
Building the system.
Zeno's successor Cleanthes, a former boxer, reportedly carried water at night to pay for his studies.
He wrote the Hymn to Zeus, one of the few early Stoic works to survive in full.
The third head, Chrysippus, was so influential that a saying went, 'If there had been no Chrysippus, there would have been no Stoa.'
Ancient sources credit him with more than 700 works, nearly all lost.
Stoic philosophy had three parts: logic, how to reason, physics, how the world works, and ethics, how to live.
They compared it to a field: logic is the fence, physics the soil, ethics the fruit.
Stoicism in Rome.
In 155 BC Athens sent three philosophers to Rome as ambassadors, including the Stoic Diogenes of Babylon, and their lectures caused a sensation.
Stoicism's focus on duty, self-control and public service suited Roman values.
Cato the Younger, who resisted Julius Caesar, became a Stoic hero.
The best-known surviving writings are from the Roman era: Seneca's letters, the teachings of Epictetus, recorded by his student Arrian, and the private notebook of Emperor Marcus Aurelius.
After about AD 200 the school faded, but its ideas lived on in Christian thought, a Renaissance revival and today's popular books, podcasts and cognitive therapies.
The key idea: Zeno lost his fortune in a shipwreck, turned to philosophy, and taught in a painted colonnade that gave Stoicism its name.
Part three. Epictetus: freedom in the mind.
Born enslaved, lame in one leg, exiled by an emperor.
Epictetus taught that no one can take away your freedom to choose your response.
Slave to teacher.
Epictetus was born around AD 50 in Hierapolis, in what is now Turkey, and enslaved from childhood.
His name means 'acquired'.
His owner, Epaphroditus, a secretary to Emperor Nero, allowed him to study Stoicism under Musonius Rufus.
He walked with a limp.
One story says his master twisted his leg until it broke while he calmly warned him it would; another says illness.
After gaining his freedom, he taught in Rome.
Around AD 93, Emperor Domitian expelled philosophers from Rome, and Epictetus opened a school at Nicopolis in Greece.
He lived simply: when a thief stole his iron lamp, he reportedly replaced it with a clay one.
He wrote nothing.
His student Arrian recorded his talks in the Discourses and the short Enchiridion, or handbook.
Control and judgement.
The Enchiridion opens with its central idea.
Within our control are our judgements, intentions, desires and actions.
Outside it are our bodies, property, reputation, other people and events.
Suffering comes from treating what we can't control as ours to command, like demanding traffic clear.
This isn't passivity: you still prepare and act, but you judge yourself by effort and character, not outcome.
Epictetus taught that 'it is not things that disturb us, but our judgements about things.'
If someone insults you, your interpretation of the insult hurts.
This idea inspired Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck as they developed rational emotive behaviour therapy and cognitive therapy.
Cognitive behavioural therapy, which grew from their work, is now among the most widely used talking therapies.
Training and roles.
Epictetus said anyone who wants to be good must train in three areas.
The first is desire: wanting only what is up to us, so we are never frustrated or afraid.
The second is action: carrying out our duties to others thoughtfully and fairly.
The third is assent: not accepting any impression as true until we've examined it, especially when tired, angry or excited.
He compared life to a play: you don't choose your role, but you can play it well.
Our duties come from our relationships as son, brother, citizen, neighbour or friend.
If your brother wrongs you, remember your role as a brother and act well anyway.
His philosophy was less abstract theory than how to behave at dinner, at work and in a family argument.
Handbook images.
The Enchiridion is full of memorable images.
Never say about anything, 'I have lost it,' Epictetus advised, but rather, 'I have given it back': possessions and even people are on loan to us.
Behave in life as at a banquet: when a dish comes round, take a modest portion politely; if it hasn't reached you yet, don't reach for it.
And don't ask for events to happen as you wish, but wish for them to happen as they do, and your life will go smoothly.
These lines are demanding, but they aim at a calm that doesn't depend on luck.
Freedom within.
For Epictetus, a formerly enslaved man, freedom meant something deep.
A tyrant could chain your leg, he said, but not even Zeus could overpower your will.
Centuries later, US Navy pilot James Stockdale was shot down over North Vietnam in 1965.

He'd been introduced to the Enchiridion while studying at Stanford, and he credited it with helping him endure more than seven years as a prisoner of war, including torture and long periods in solitary confinement.
As he parachuted down, he later wrote, he told himself he was leaving the world of technology and entering the world of Epictetus.
The key idea: Epictetus was born enslaved, gained his freedom and taught philosophy, first in Rome and then in Nicopolis.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. How did books like Irvine's and Holiday's change Stoicism's reputation?
Answer. They presented it as a practical philosophy for ordinary people.
Question two. What did Zeno mean by joking that he had made a prosperous voyage when shipwrecked?
Answer. Losing his cargo led him to philosophy.
Question three. What did Epictetus's life show about his philosophy?
Answer. Mental freedom survives any circumstances.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
